What you said
- Structure: 1/3 — you name the action but not the context or result.
- Evidence: 0/3 — no outcome, numbers or impact.

You don't have any Lincoln International interview items on file yet. The one step that starts a tracked prep is: paste the interview invite or the posting (or tell me the round format, length, and who you'll meet). I'll save it and use it to make a tailored plan.

Quick targeted prep for a final-round analyst interview at Lincoln International (M&A / middle-market):
What they want to hear, in short
- You can do core technical work (financial statements, valuation basics, deal math).  
- You understand the M&A process and an analyst’s role on deals.  
- You can think commercially about value drivers and risks.  
- You communicate clearly, prioritize, and take ownership under tight deadlines.  
- You fit the team: professional, detail-oriented, proactive.
10‑point prep plan (do these in order; allow 2–3 hours total if you already know the basics)
1) Read the invite/posting and note interviewer names & titles — tailor your answers to show deal exposure and sector interest. (Paste it so I can save it.)
2) Prepare a 2–3 minute “Walk me through your resume” that links your experience to deal work and ends with why Lincoln specifically.
3) STAR stories: prepare 4 short behavioral answers (60–90s): a time you handled an error/missed deadline, led on a team, prioritized multiple tasks, and showed initiative that improved a process. Include the action you took and the measurable result or lesson.
4) DCF walk-through: practice a crisp, step-by-step DCF in 90–120s (forecast FCF, discount with WACC, choose terminal method, sum PVs, reconcile to equity value). Be ready to explain sensitivities.
5) Comps & precedent logic: explain when and why you use comps vs. precedent transactions and how you pick multiples. Be ready to justify chosen peers/metrics.
6) Enterprise vs equity value: state the formula and list common adjustments (debt, cash, minorities, unfunded pensions, etc.).
7) Quick case drill (5–8 min): structure an answer: clarify objective, summarize facts, identify 3 value drivers, outline risks/mitigants, give recommendation and next analyses. Time yourself.
8) One short modeling check: be ready to do back-of-envelope math (margin to EBITDA, simple accretion/dilution logic, sensitivity to multiple or margin changes). Practice two quick calculations aloud.
9) Prepare 3–5 smart questions to ask them (mix deal-specific and career/culture): e.g., types of deals in year 1; how analysts get client exposure; an interesting recent deal and why it was attractive.
10) Logistics & final polish: confirm interview length and format, print one-page cheat sheet of your deals/STAR bullets (if allowed), rest well, and plan a 1–2 sentence closing that reiterates fit and interest.
Core sample questions to practice (answer aloud, time yourself)
- Walk me through your resume. (2–3 min)  
- Why Lincoln International? Why this sector/team? (60–90s)  
- Tell me about a time you missed a deadline or made an error. What happened and what did you do? (STAR)  
- Walk me through a DCF. (90–120s)  
- How do you calculate WACC and what moves it? (60–90s)  
- How would you value a company with negative cash flows? (60–90s)  
- Here’s a short company — would you advise the client to sell? (structure, 3–6 min)
Two short practice drills to run now
- Drill A (3–5 min): Given revenue, margin, and a simple buyer multiple, sketch the 3‑year sensitivity if margin improves by X points. State the impact on EBITDA and whether sale becomes attractive.  
- Drill B (5–8 min): Given a target EBITDA and a range of market multiples, produce a quick valuation range and recommend an opening negotiation stance, noting key assumptions.

Scoring tips for answers
- Structure first (what you’ll say), then evidence (concrete action you did), then a short quantified result or lesson.  
- For technical answers, name the steps first, then run one quick example to show you can do the math.
Interview micro-tips
- Use interviewer names, mirror energy, and pause to let them redirect if you outline a long structure.  
- If given an on-the-spot case, outline your approach aloud before diving into numbers.  
- Keep behavioral answers tight: situation, your action, outcome (with a number if possible), then brief learning.  
- End with a short summary of fit and one question about next steps.

If you want, we can run a mock final round now: tell me the interview format (behavioral, technical, case; length) and who you’ll meet (titles). I’ll ask the first question and score your answer.

Is that right?
